paras: The threatened lynching of William Dieckman took place at Hilltown, St. Louis County, Missouri, on March 17, 1881, when 75 to 100 farmers gathered intending to lynch Dieckman, who was jailed for the fatal stabbing of his employer, Henry W. Mertz. No attack on the prisoner was reported, and in July he was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to 18 years. Papers from Wheeling to Dallas carried the story, one under the headline "Threatened Lynching."

Mertz was the postmaster at Hilltown, a settlement on the Olive Street road twenty miles west of St. Louis and off any railroad. According to a St. Louis wire, on the evening of Monday, March 14, Dieckman had an altercation with Mertz that led to a fight, and stabbed him in the abdomen and thigh. The Post-Dispatch account alleged that Dieckman had threatened murder beforehand and had been seen sharpening his knife, remarking, "This will bring blood." He was captured some hours later and locked up in the jail at Clayton.

Feeling against Dieckman was sharpened by an older case: his wife had been murdered at Hog Hollow two years earlier. The wire said a man named Stoeckli had been convicted of that crime but that many believed Dieckman was the real murderer, while the Post-Dispatch said Dieckman had first been suspected and Stoeckli had since been tried twice.

Mertz died of his wounds in the night of March 16-17, by the Post-Dispatch's account at about four in the morning. As the news spread, farmers gathered from the surrounding country, and between 75 and 100 were at Hilltown and Lake post-office that morning. The Post-Dispatch messenger reported "but one sentiment" among them, that Dieckman deserved death, and wrote that there was "a strong prospect" he would not live to see sundown.

Constable Kessler and his deputy, Jake Berg, were reported to have left for Clayton to bring the prisoner to Hilltown about noon for the inquest, which 'Squires Fischer and Reaves had been notified to hold. A further fifty men were rumored to be coming from Manchester and Baldwin. The "more hot-headed" favored taking Dieckman from the posse at Lake post-office and lynching him before the inquest, while others counseled waiting for the verdict.

No report of an attack on the prisoner or of the inquest verdict appears in the coverage. Dieckman, spelled "Keokman" in a July 1 dispatch, was tried for four days at Clayton for killing Mertz. The jury returned a verdict of murder in the second degree and fixed his punishment at 18 years in the penitentiary.

The story reached most papers through a St. Louis wire dated March 17, printed the next day in the Memphis Appeal, both Wheeling dailies and the Chicago Tribune. Headlines differed: the Wheeling Register ran "Threatened Lynching. A Mob Assembling to Seek Vengeance," the Wheeling Intelligencer "Dierkman's Dark Deeds," and the Memphis Appeal a head that read, through garbled type, "Evidently Deserves Hanging." Shorter items in the New-York Tribune and the Memphis Public Ledger reported only the stabbing.

A fuller account from a Post-Dispatch messenger ran as a special dispatch in the Chicago Tribune on March 18 and, credited to the Post-Dispatch, in the Dallas Herald on March 22 under "Possibly a Lynching." It relayed the crowd's view of Dieckman without comment and closed with his alleged knife remark. None of the reports gave the race of Dieckman or Mertz.

bases: Farmers gathered at Hilltown with the stated aim of seizing the jailed prisoner from officers and lynching him, a threatened lynching that was not carried out; he was later tried and imprisoned (A1, A4, A8, A9).

A crowd of 75 to 100 men talked of taking Dieckman from the posse and lynching him for the killing of Mertz (A4, A8), but no attack is reported and in July he was tried and sentenced to 18 years for the killing (A9), so no one was killed.
The St. Louis wire (A1, A6, A7) and the separate Post-Dispatch account (A4, A8) independently report the gathering to lynch him, and a July report confirms the stabbing and his trial (A9).

accounts.gist: Seventy-five to a hundred farmers gathered as officers prepared to bring Dieckman from Clayton for the inquest; the 'more hot-headed' wanted to seize him en route, others to wait for the verdict.

accounts.label: Trial report
accounts.gist: Dieckman was tried at Clayton, convicted of second-degree murder and given 18 years.

framing.detail: The wire ran under varied heads, from the Wheeling Register's 'Threatened Lynching' to the Memphis Appeal's garbled 'Evidently Deserves Hanging', and said the case was 'aggravated' by suspicion over his wife's death.

record_check.dossier: One man, William Dieckman, under several spellings (Dreckman, Dierkman, Dieckman, Keokman).
No paper states the race of Dieckman or Mertz; nothing in the coverage shows this as anti-Black violence.
Neighbors of Mertz and farmers of western St. Louis County, 75 to 100 men.
Held in the Clayton jail; officers were to bring him to Hilltown for the inquest. Later tried and convicted (18 years).

info: Mertz was stabbed on Monday, March 14, 1881; he died on the night of March 16 or early on March 17; the crowd gathered at Hilltown on the morning of March 17.
Hilltown, on the Olive Street road, twenty miles west of St. Louis, off any railroad; men also gathered at Lake post-office.
William Dieckman (spelled Dreckman, Dierkman, Dickman, Dieckmaa, Keokman), the targeted prisoner; no race is stated in any report.

Accused of fatally stabbing his employer Henry W. Mertz, Hilltown's postmaster, in the abdomen and thigh after an altercation; some neighbors also suspected him in his wife's murder two years earlier.
Neighbors of Mertz and farmers from the surrounding country; a further body of fifty men was reported coming from Manchester and Baldwin.
Convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to 18 years in the penitentiary.
